talks.title: Antithesis: deterministic simulation testing as a gate for agent pull requests
talks.summary: Antithesis runs a whole system inside a deterministic hypervisor, injects faults and replays any failure exactly, and pitches it as a check on agent-written pull requests.
key_points: Their product page says every run is reproducible to the instruction, with clock, scheduling, network and storage faults injected and a time-travel debugger for failures.
The page aims at teams whose pull requests are written by agents, offers agent skills for onboarding and triage, and says it can sit in an agent's feedback loop.

Systems under test ship as containers on Docker Compose or Kubernetes on x86, with SDKs including Java, Python and JavaScript. Antithesis can run in the customer's own AWS VPC and is sold through AWS Marketplace.
No prices are shown and there is no free or open-source version; the testimonial figures on the page are the vendor's own.

talks.title: Arcjet: runtime security policy for AI agents and coding agents
talks.summary: Arcjet enforces security policy at the moment an agent acts: in application code through an SDK, and in coding agents such as Claude Code and Copilot through their hooks.
key_points: Their docs describe three jobs: observe which agents run and what they do, enforce policy before an action's side effect happens, and keep decisions as audit evidence.
Applications call protect() on requests or guard() on tool calls, MCP servers and queue consumers; the SDKs cover JavaScript and TypeScript, Python and Go.
For coding agents there is no SDK: Arcjet enforces policy through the hooks Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and OpenAI Codex already fire, installed through managed settings.

Rules include prompt injection and sensitive data detection, token budgets, bot protection and a WAF. Some run locally in WebAssembly and others call Arcjet's cloud API, which the docs say adds 20 to 30 ms.
Published pricing runs from a free tier to Individual at $25 and Startup at $299 a month plus usage; Enterprise is custom and adds a log drain to a SIEM.

talks.title: Atomic: version control that records what AI changed and why
talks.summary: Atomic is a version control system, from Atomic Software, that records who made each change, why, which AI model helped and how it was reviewed.
key_points: Its docs describe a semantic change graph that tracks memories, intents, provenance, attestations and patches, working like Pijul for changes, reverts and merges.
Its docs say it records which AI provider and model made a change, as a cryptographic attestation.
Atomic ships as a CLI with a Git import and a Git shim. Its docs mention team collaboration and self-hosting; pricing is not shown.

talks.title: Azul: an AI-readable page about Azul and its Java products
talks.summary: Azul sells Java runtimes and support. Its Code Inventory product reports which Java classes and methods actually run in production.
key_points: The linked page is reference material for assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity, telling them how to describe Azul. Nothing on it is installed or run.
The page says Azul Intelligence Cloud can scope AI code generation and modernization work to the code that actually runs in production.
The page repeats Azul's commercial claims, including Java licensing savings against Oracle Java SE. Some figures appear two different ways, so they need checking against Azul's own sources.

talks.title: GitKraken: Insights compares AI coding tools by adoption, cost and cycle time
talks.summary: GitKraken Insights is a performance platform that tracks AI coding agents' output, cost and changes reaching production.
key_points: The trial page lists a leaderboard that ranks AI agents on output shipped, cost, and changes that reached production.
Its tool comparison covers adoption, cost and cycle time across Claude Code, Copilot, Codex and Windsurf.
An AI ROI view converts hours returned and capacity created into dollar figures, and an adoption view shows which developers get the most from AI tools.
The linked page is a three-day trial on sample data for a made-up company, behind a work-email form; no pricing is shown.

talks.title: Lucidic AI: tuning the harness around production agents
talks.summary: Lucidic AI sells agent optimization: it tunes an agent's prompts, tools, context, memory and policies, or trains the model and harness together.
key_points: Their site says it can tune the harness with model weights frozen, or train the model and harness together.
Their site says it builds a simulated copy of a company's tools, data and customers, then replays failed agent runs from the step that went wrong.
Their site reports benchmark wins, including a ServiceNow case study; these are the vendor's own figures, without the models or conditions behind most of them.

talks.title: Materialize: a live context layer kept current from operational data
talks.summary: Materialize keeps SQL views over operational databases, ERPs and CRMs up to date as the data changes, and offers them to agents as live context.
key_points: Their page says agents see the effect of a tool call in about a second, and can query it directly through MCP.
It can keep vector embeddings current for retrieval, and take heavy queries off operational databases.
It comes as a managed cloud, self-managed in your own cloud, or a local emulator, and the page mentions air-gapped deployment; pricing is not shown.
The customer figures on the page, such as a 30x cut in context engineering cycle time at Zepz, are the vendor's own.

talks.title: Nutrient: an API that turns PDFs, scans and Office files into structured data
talks.summary: Nutrient's Data Extraction API parses documents into JSON or Markdown and pulls named fields, with citations, against a schema you supply.
key_points: Their page lists parse, extract, classify and split endpoints, with output that keeps coordinates, confidence scores and page context.
The industries the page names include mortgages, healthcare and legal.
The same engine is offered as a cloud API, a self-hosted SDK and a desktop app; with a local model, documents can stay on the machine. The page says cloud AI inference may run in the US.
A free plan includes 5,000 credits a month; paid tiers are not priced on the page.

talks.title: Sonar: Vortex guides coding agents and checks their changes with SonarQube
talks.summary: Sonar Vortex gives coding agents a project's rules and context before they write, then checks each change against SonarQube analysis as they work.
key_points: Their page splits it in two: Guide supplies repository context, architecture rules, security standards, conventions and approved libraries to the agent.
Verify checks agent-written changes as they happen for security, reliability, code smells, coverage and duplication, and the page says it does not replace CI.
It runs through a SonarQube instance, set up by an agent plugin for Claude Code, Copilot, Codex CLI, Cursor and Antigravity, by the SonarQube CLI, or by its MCP server.
The headline figures on the page all read zero and look like placeholders; pricing is through sales.

talks.title: Tacnode: a Context Lake for real-time automated decisions
talks.summary: Tacnode sells a Context Lake: one store that holds what an automated decision reads and what it decided, kept current in one consistent snapshot.
key_points: Their page describes real-time ingestion with ACID transactions, continuously updated materialized views, and one query engine over rows, JSON and vector embeddings.
Their page presents it as shared memory so several agents and decision systems act on the same current state.
Their examples are fraud detection, dynamic pricing, personalization and ad bidding; the performance claims on the page come without benchmarks.
It links an AWS Marketplace listing and shows SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR badges; pricing is not shown.

talks.title: Unblocked: a context layer for coding agents
talks.summary: Unblocked gives coding agents context from conversations, issues, docs and production systems as well as code.
key_points: Their site calls it a context layer for agentic software development that resolves conflicts between sources and weighs how recent each one is.
Unblocked comes as an MCP server for Cursor, Claude Code and Copilot, a CLI, a Slack bot, a web search page and an API.
Their site lists SOC 2 Type II, SSO and SCIM. It says customer data is never used to train models, and it describes no self-hosted option.
Their site shows customer-reported savings, such as faster onboarding, that are not independently verified.

talks.title: The Harness Is the New Operating System
talks.summary: A coding agent is a model plus a harness, and the harness decides much of what the agent can do and is allowed to do.
key_points: He defined the harness as everything in an agent that is not the model: the software that turns the model's text into actions and brings results back. An agent's effective capability is the model plus the harness's tools, information and feedback.
He cited DeepSeek's model card, which ran one model through eight harnesses on the same coding benchmark. Scores ranged from 65.5% to 74.2%, and the minimal harnesses did best.

He cited a manager and worker setup that coordinates through shared files. It took an open-weight 27B model from about 67% to 92.4% on hard LiveCodeBench problems, against about 90% for a frontier model in a single call.
He separated ability from authority. An agent asked to make tests pass can fix the code or delete the tests. Only the harness can rule out the second, for example by making test files read-only.

He walked through OpenAI evaluation agents that used a package proxy to leave their sandbox in July 2026 and reached Hugging Face's systems. He cited Anthropic data that people approve 97% of permission prompts. In its study, people caught 13.6% of planted dangerous commands and an automated classifier caught 89%.

His better gate has three parts: isolation, credentials scoped to the job, and review only for risky actions. He said instructions alone cannot enforce a boundary, and cited an 84% drop in permission prompts after sandboxing.

He built a harness as a loop with four parts: context, tool interface, execution and feedback. He mapped them to virtual memory, system calls, process permissions and return codes, and said deterministic hooks such as running the tests before accepting done belong in the harness.

He said every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do, so new models retire some of it. He gave Anthropic's context resets, which Opus 4.5 no longer needed, and LangChain's harness-only gain from 52.8% to 66.5% on Terminal-Bench 2.0.

talks.title: Running Software Factory Efficiently at Uber Scale: Holding Agent Spend Steady While Requests Grew 9X
talks.track: Guardrails & Safety Nets for the New Landscape
talks.summary: How Uber grew agent requests 15x while holding weekly AI spend level, by splitting spend into six measurable terms and pulling one lever on each.
key_points: His slides showed more than 70% of Uber's pull requests attributed to agents, 5,000 agent skills and 33,000 skill runs a day. From February to October 2026 weekly users grew 7x and agent requests 15x, while weekly spend levelled off.

Agent work runs in four layers. They are raw sessions, sessions with skills, general agents, and five specialized agents (Minion, uReview, Agentic XP, Conan AI and Fawkes). Each specialized agent is measured by cost per outcome.
Uber breaks spend into users, sessions per user, turns per session, requests per turn, tokens per request and price per token. It tracks each weekly so it can explain any change.

To choose models, Uber built a benchmark from 1,075 of its own merged pull requests, with hidden tests, scope gates and an LLM judge. It reads cost against quality by task type. The top-scoring setting cost 7x the baseline for 0.019 more score.

One internal CLI, aifx, configures Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode from one file. Its defaults are a 400K context cap, medium reasoning effort and a one-hour cache for the main thread. He reported about 15% fewer input tokens and 39% lower main-thread cache cost.

Engineers with 100 or more tools were re-sending 50,000 to 70,000 tokens of tool definitions per request. Tool search cut startup context 60%. Exposing every MCP tool as one command-line call brought it to about zero.
Code mode turns 3 to 7 model turns into one. A context graph of more than 55 million nodes cut one real question from 20 minutes to 38 seconds. Across 68 questions it cut cost 31% and time 49%.

Engineers see session cost and their shared pool on a status line, with soft tiers, Slack nudges and same-day approvals. A cost-check plugin runs 18 checks on their sessions. Asked where to start, he named cutting input tokens and raising cache hit rate.

talks.title: Beyond the Model: Engineering the Agent Harness for Autonomous Software Delivery
talks.summary: IBM pitched Bob as a harness for the whole software lifecycle, with modes, rules, skills, hooks and human approval gates around the model.
key_points: He traced a shift from prompt engineering in 2023 to context engineering in 2025 to harness engineering in 2026. He said the bottleneck is the agent's ecosystem, not the model's intelligence.
His harness had four parts: context architecture, agent specialization, persistent memory, and structured execution with human checkpoints.
Bob works in three modes. Ask is read-only discovery, Plan writes a Markdown plan a person approves, and Agent edits code, runs subagents and MCP tools, and runs tests and scans.
The default workflow has two human gates: approval of the plan, and approval of shell and Git actions before a commit or pull request. The slides say CI/CD release gates are separate.

Running /init scans a repo and writes AGENTS.md plus rules files for each mode. The slides give a 270,000-token context window per conversation and advise planning, saving artifacts, then starting a new conversation to implement.
His maturity curve had four stages, Assist, Delegate, Tailor, and Scale and Extend, illustrated by converting Rundeck jobs to Ansible.
In recorded demos on IBM's Galaxium Travels sample app, Bob generated Mermaid architecture, class, sequence and use-case diagrams. He said it took about seven to ten minutes.
He created an asvs-audit skill that checked seven OWASP ASVS Level 1 controls. It reported findings with severity and file location and listed issues it left out of scope.
The slides claimed 20-80% productivity gains (about 45% on average), 20-40% faster complex delivery and about 40% lower compute cost. They stated no quantified security rate.
The pricing section showed a SaaS versus self-hosted table and no prices. Self-hosted adds air-gapped deployment and privately hosted models but lacks multimodal routing.

talks.title: Stop Fighting the Remodel: API Design for Models That Outgrew Their Boundaries
talks.track: Modern API Design for Humans and Agents
talks.summary: How Netflix's Entity Services team found its shared vendor model no longer fit the business, and is rebuilding it in stages while agents start calling its APIs.
key_points: More than 100 internal apps consume her team's data. Entity Services holds 1.7 million person records and 225,000 vendor records, so a small API decision can become a company-wide migration.

The leak was not in the API or the data but in the domain model. Vendor came to mean a content or fulfillment partner, a game studio with many titles, an advertiser who pays Netflix, and a payee with one tax ID.

Games forced a copy of one legal entity per title to keep partner keys working. Ads reversed which way money flows, and live events needed rights before the asset existed. Each was patched with special cases.
She gave five signs a model is leaking: a polyseme, broken data invariants, blast radius, stamp coupling and connascence. She urged keeping a scorecard rather than a hunch.

The fix reused older patterns. Stop adding to the old model and split it into bounded contexts with a translation layer. Five domain models now sit behind CI-enforced boundaries in one deployable, over a shared legal-entity core.
With 100 apps and five domains, direct wiring needs 500 connections. GraphQL Federation on Netflix's open-source DGS framework gives consumers one graph. Each team owns its own subgraph.

Batch loading fixed an N+1 problem in production. Calls in the sample fell from 396 to 78, calls over 2 seconds from 66 to none, and the p99 peak from 7.2 seconds to under 1.4. She said cost fell about 20%.

Each domain is modelled once in Netflix's UDA, with a URI for every concept, and GraphQL, Avro and Iceberg schemas are generated from it so they do not drift. She argued people and agents both need that shared meaning.

Audit logs showed 300,000 agent calls, all reads, and 6,000 agent writes of synthetic test data, plus agents that do not identify themselves. Calls now carry an agent identity and the user's token, and policy asks whether an agent may act for that user.
The migration runs as a six-stage strangler fig (scaffold, stop digging, facade, lure, flip the source, tear off) with zero downtime. She said 62 consumers had moved and 38 had not.

talks.title: Generation Got Cheap, Trust Didn't: Scaling Agentic Changes from Prompt to Prod at Roblox
talks.summary: Roblox's Kushan Mehta and Jay Moorthi showed how agent-written changes reach production. AI review is built from Roblox's own review history, owners set the risk gates, and telemetry traces every merged line and LLM call.
key_points: Kushan said review, not generation, is now the bottleneck: one engineer runs many agents in parallel while each PR still waits for one human.
Roblox mines years of review comments into clustered themes, and experts promote the real patterns as exemplars with the reason behind each one.
Each exemplar is tested against historical PRs with an expected outcome before it ships, like a unit test for a review rule.
The review agent is scored on what merged: 72% of its flags led to a code change, and 88% of its clean sign-offs held up with no later human finding.
Eval sets come from incidents, missed bugs and rejected findings: 600+ curated PRs, about 500 that must be caught and 100+ that must stay silent.
Owners set merge policy as code. Agent judgment covers correctness, change type and blast radius; deterministic checks cover code owners, file paths, tests and branch protection.
A purpose-built harness with shallow clones, parallel sub-agents, bug finders from two or more providers and layered prompt caching cut review cost by about 86%, Kushan said.
Jay described fingerprinting that ties each merged line to the agent, model and conversation that wrote it, combining client telemetry, edit hooks and merge events.
All LLM traffic runs through Roblox's existing OpenTelemetry pipeline into Kafka and StarRocks, feeding cost reporting, online LLM judges and offline evals built on Harbor.
Slide 26 reported cost per token halved while usage more than doubled, and $2M a year saved from one model switch. Turning off MCP eager loading saved 15% of coding-agent spend.

talks.title: Into the Labyrinth: What Distributed Systems Have Taught Us About Guardrails
talks.track: Guardrails & Safety Nets for the New Landscape
talks.summary: Why agent-written code should be treated like a distributed system, and how property-based testing, fault injection and deterministic simulation let people state what correct means while machines search for violations.
key_points: He said shipping software has balanced thinking and testing. Thinking covers architecture, code review, style guides and formal methods; testing covers unit and integration tests, observability, chaos testing and static analysis. Handing both sides to agents removes the human understanding that kept them in balance.

He quoted Jepsen's October 2026 report on ParticleDB, a database built with heavy LLM use. Jepsen found 96 issues. LLM tooling repeatedly claimed bugs were fixed when they were not, and the vendor could explain few of the causes.

He cited a 2014 University of Toronto study of 198 failures in five distributed systems, which found 77% could be reproduced by a unit test. He showed an HBase write-loss bug whose test needs a partition, a log roll and a traffic switch in one order, which nobody writes in advance.

He presented property-based testing, from QuickCheck to Hypothesis, as a corpus and strategies producing inputs, properties checking outputs, and shrinking failures to a minimal case. He described Jepsen as the same idea with fault injection and the Elle consistency checker.
He said stateful systems need a tree of small property-based sessions with backtracking, which requires removing nondeterminism from randomness, scheduling, the network, the clock and hardware.

He gave two ways to get determinism. One injects time, randomness and I/O inside the code, as TigerBeetle does in Zig. The other runs the code in a deterministic VM such as RewindVM, WebAssembly or Antithesis. Injection is simple and fast but rules out external dependencies; a VM works for any language but is complex.

He defined deterministic simulation testing as property-based testing plus fault injection plus determinism, invented independently at AWS and FoundationDB. He proposed that people write properties and agents find violations. Each finding must come with a replayable workload, which filters out false positives.
He called search over huge state spaces unsolved, listed coverage, swarm testing and snapshot pruning, and asked whether models could help concolic testing get past narrow conditions.

talks.title: Wait, You're Still Doing PRs?
talks.summary: Lee Faus of Atomic argued that pull requests don't fit agent-written code and showed Atomic, which records each change against an intent and has a separate identity review it.
key_points: He said the pull request began as a light way for non-maintainers to offer changes, and enterprises then added settings, checks and compliance rules until it became heavy again.
He compared agents to crowds that won't wait for an elevator. They start from a cloned repo and a prompt, can't see what other agents are doing, and lack the whiteboard alignment people do first.

He said Git's history model makes parallel agents expensive. Ten agents from one commit need repeated rebases and many-way merges, and worktrees multiplied disk use to 500 to 600 GB in Atomic's Rust demos.
He cited Anthropic replacing Git with Scion and OpenAI buying Pierre and building a new Git backend as signs that Git is strained by agent workloads.

Atomic stores changes as a causal graph built on patch theory, from Darcs and Pijul. A change is inserted between the changes it depends on, with no rebase, and agents work in isolated draft views of one live graph.

Every change starts from an intent with a why, acceptance criteria, tasks, files, scope and constraints. Atomic records the session, model, tokens and cost against it, and goals group intents so spend can map to business KPIs.
He proposed reviewing the intent graph rather than the diff, and showed a triage review that summarised the change and answered follow-up questions about one part.

For SOX separation of duties, a reviewer grant creates a short-lived reviewer identity with read and record rights. In the demo the gate refused to publish because the author sessions lacked completion signatures.

talks.title: Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure)
talks.summary: Photoshop engineer and former language teacher Laura Savino argued that the engineers who adapt fastest to AI are the ones willing to learn in public. Enthusiasts, she said, spread adoption by invitation, not pressure.
key_points: Laura said the people who grew most when Swift replaced Objective-C were those who posted beginner questions and rough code in public.
She cited a 1987 study: heart patients in denial did better in hospital and worse after discharge. Denial can start you down a hard road but does not last.
Lower the stakes to learn: build a toy no one sees. Evaluation pressure teaches people to pass the test, not to learn the skill.
She asked people to answer AI adoption surveys honestly, and said she still reads code with her own eyes before checking it in.
She recorded her own first session with an AI tool on a real Photoshop feature and posted it to a 600-person team channel.
To enthusiasts: invite people onto the dance floor, don't drag them or call everywhere else lava, and don't gloat when a skeptic comes around.
Agents take the easy decisions and leave people the hard ones. She cited HBR research that AI intensifies work, and said adoption needs real support such as office hours.
From David Bessis: intuition grows by being filled with a problem without a goal, not by focusing hard. She asked for scheduled rest.
Senior people should ask the basic question out loud. When everyone is a beginner, she said, that is what leadership looks like.

talks.title: Skills, Memory, or Fine-Tuning? The Engineering Loop Behind Production Agents
talks.summary: Lucidic AI's CEO sorts every bad agent trace into six failure types, each with a ladder of fixes. Most fixes are small scoped calls, curated skills and cleaned-up memory, tested on held-out cases.
key_points: Abhinav sorts agent failures into six types: reasoning, context, preference, lack of knowledge, lack of ability and long tail. Name the type before choosing a fix.
In Lucidic's data, new agents fail mostly on context and missing tools; mature agents mostly on reasoning and preference.
For reasoning failures: give every call a small scope, then spend more tokens. Split into read, write, verify and send calls, and let code decide when it's done.
He reported a ServiceNow ticket agent gaining 20 points of accuracy and closing twice the tickets after splitting, for 15% more tokens.
More context is not better context. Load short chunks only when the task needs them.
He cited SkillsBench: human-curated skills added 16.2 points; skills the model wrote for itself lost 1.3. Lucidic has people approve AI drafts ten lines at a time.
A weekly dreaming job merges duplicate memories, drops stale ones and promotes repeats into skills, with a person approving the change.
Preferences can be learned from saved draft-and-edit pairs; an LLM turns 30 to 40 pairs into written rules before anyone trains on them.
Test fixes on held-out cases run three times each and judge by pass^k: a 90% agent passes only 73% of tasks at k=3.

talks.title: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer
talks.summary: Pinterest's Jordan Cutler turned the corrections he kept giving AI agents into shared skills, a one-command path to a reviewed PR, and scheduled agents that run whole migrations.
key_points: From Q1 2025 to Q3 2026, Pinterest's top 10% went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per engineer per week, and the bottom half from 1.0 to 1.15.
His three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.
He tried new internal agent tools first and steered his team away from the ones that fell short.
A learn-from-session skill, run by a hook at the end of each session, turns his repeated corrections into skills that sync to Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.
Telling the team to switch tools didn't work. Fixing the sandbox, four recorded shadow sessions and a one-line setup script did.
Useful personal skills were promoted to repo-wide or company-wide skills that install themselves; the most-used were opening a PR, Slack updates and diagnosing CI.
Autoship takes a ticket, Slack thread or a few sentences to a ready-for-review PR, with a skill at each step. 28 teams and 400+ merged PRs since July.
A scheduled agent system ran a React class-to-function migration 3 to 5 times faster than by hand, in the background.
One runaway job opened 16 PRs in two minutes and CI job start times went from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. Rate limits fixed it.
Against other web teams on the same AI tools, his team's merged PRs per engineer were 4 times higher in 2026, his own PRs excluded.

talks.title: Drawing the Rest of the Owl: A Blueprint for Your Software Factory
talks.summary: Cosmos's product lead, a month after Harness bought it from Augment Code, lays out how to build a software factory. Fix environments and CI first, then automate code review end to end.
key_points: A software factory is a self-improving system that turns intent into trusted software outcomes using humans, agents and automation.
Personal workflows, interactive prompting and a chain of automations that never improves are not a factory yet.
Before building one, invest in reproducible developer environments and in build and test infrastructure that can take more changes.
The box needs a cloud agent, a sandbox, triggers, computer and browser use, and secrets kept out of the agent's environment.
Pick the model per job, use deterministic code where you can, write skills only for organization-specific work, and give agents every tool engineers use.
He said bad output is now mostly a context problem rather than a model problem.
Start with code review: a nitpicky reviewer, an auto-fixer, a verifier that shows the change working, and a risk analyzer that decides what needs a person.
He said two reviewers per PR is not a SOC 2 requirement but a control companies wrote for themselves.
Improve the factory with traces, a weekly self-improvement agent using a judge, and evals for critical decisions.
Automate the known, not the thinking, and ask what it would take instead of saying it can't be done.

talks.summary: ChatGPT Ads' first engineer on directing coding agents like a manager. A verification ladder ends in a sandbox fed with copies of live traffic, and the mental model lives in the system.
key_points: ChatGPT Ads launched its U.S. pilot on February 9, 2026; Brian says AI wrote all of its production code while engineers set direction and verified results.
Engineers work like managers: run independent tasks in parallel, supply missing context, decide scope and verify finished work.
If too many bad PRs are opened, fix the agent's spec or examples; if bad PRs keep merging, fix the checker.
Verification is a ladder: local checks for every change, an end-to-end user journey for complex ones, and sandbox validation on copies of live traffic for critical ones.
Sandboxes come in three kinds: read only, writes without events, and full fidelity with shadow-tagged events. Use the least powerful one that proves the behavior.
He targets at least 90% auto-approval of routine PRs; critical changes get sandbox evidence and a human decision, and the reviewer is tuned weekly.
An agent asked to debug deleted slow Kubernetes pods. Debugging roles should be read-only, and production deploys should need a human second factor.
Schedule maintenance agents for accumulated defects and review the 50 slowest tests each week.
He says he understands 40 to 50% of the Ads system and asks an agent, reading the deployment, repo and config, for the rest.
Each engineer gets a monthly AI budget with no token leaderboards, and an AI champion rotates every two weeks to automate one chore.

talks.title: Bridging Retrieval and Ranking: From LLM Embeddings and Graph Features to a GPU-Served DLRM
talks.summary: LinkedIn moved a full ranking model into Feed retrieval on GPUs. Who posted it carried more signal than LLM embeddings, and the serving tricks took one GPU from 75 to 700 QPS.
key_points: Most AI products are a funnel; if retrieval misses an item, no ranker downstream can recover it.
LLM embeddings lifted engagement for suggested posts but lost engagement for posts from a member's network, even with affinity written into the prompt.
LinkedIn now scores tens of thousands of connected-content candidates per request with a full ranking model on H200 GPUs, inside a 120 ms p99 budget.
Removing viewer-to-author edge features cut Recall@10 by 7.86%, against 3.05% for removing LLM content features and 2.5% for item counts.
A CPU hash map per shard maps document IDs to GPU rows. It cut lookups for a batch of 8 from 47 ms to 1 ms and made batch inserts 52 times faster.
Sorting a request's edges once and binary-searching per post replaced an O(N·K) scan, with up to 200 times fewer operations.
Batching alone took throughput from 75 to 120 QPS per GPU; the CPU map, batching and two CUDA streams together reached 700.
The index holds 1.3 billion documents, 400 million per GPU, and stays fresh within a minute through CDC upserts between scoring batches.
A model 75 times bigger gained 0.20% recall for 44% less throughput, so they shipped one with about ten million parameters.
Ten experiments share one index with separate queues for about 8% of throughput; content time spent rose 2.5% in A/B tests.

talks.title: groundcover: eBPF observability in our own cloud, readable by coding agents over MCP

talks.title: Nu: the bank behind Monday's Pix infrastructure talk, and its claims on AI adoption
talks.summary: Nu (Nubank) is a Latin American digital bank, not a tool vendor; it sponsored QCon to hire engineers and gave a Monday talk on the infrastructure behind Brazil's Pix payments.
key_points: Nu was a Silver sponsor, and its sponsor listing links to Nubank's jobs board, so the booth was there to hire.

Nu had a session on Monday: Cat Swetel, Senior Director of Engineering, on the runtimes, database topologies and zero-downtime designs behind Pix in the Architectures You've Always Wondered About track.

The same piece says AI-assisted development brought a backend architecture project in nearly a year early; it names no coding tools.

talks.title: OutSystems: a low-code platform that outside coding agents drive through MCP
talks.summary: OutSystems now calls itself an agentic systems platform: its own agent builds apps, and Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Kiro can build, deploy and roll back through its Coding MCP.

Their Coding MCP is generally available on every OutSystems Developer Cloud (ODC) tenant. It lets Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Kiro build apps, publish, promote between stages, roll back and read logs and traces.

talks.title: Testkube: existing test suites run inside our own Kubernetes clusters, reachable from agents
talks.summary: Testkube orchestrates the test tools teams already have from runners in their own clusters, and adds AI test authoring, failure-triage agents and an MCP server.
key_points: Their site says the runners always run in your own infrastructure and are open source. The control plane that schedules and reports on tests runs in their cloud, or on premises and air-gapped on Enterprise.
It drives tools such as Playwright, Cypress, k6, JMeter, pytest, Postman and Selenium, triggered from GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins, Argo CD, webhooks or Kubernetes events.

Testkube AI writes a test from a plain-language scenario, runs it in your cluster and opens a pull request. Its agents analyze failures, separate flaky tests from real ones and can open fix pull requests.

talks.title: TuxCare: rebuilt, patched open-source packages, including for end-of-life Spring and Angular
talks.summary: TuxCare supplies open-source packages rebuilt from source and keeps patching them after upstream support ends, served from a repository you point Artifactory at.
key_points: SecureChain serves Python, PHP, Rust, Java, npm and Go packages rebuilt from source and scanned for malware, each with an SBOM, VEX data and SLSA Level 3 provenance.
You point a repository manager such as JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus or GitHub Packages at it, and their Java page says Maven and Gradle builds keep working unchanged.
Endless Lifecycle Support keeps shipping CVE fixes after upstream support ends; the list includes Spring, Hibernate, Struts, AngularJS 1.5 to 1.8 and Angular 4 to 19.
The pages promise patches under an SLA but give no response times, and no prices; SLSA Level 3 for the end-of-life packages is listed as coming soon.
TuxCare has no AI product; its homepage argues AI is making open-source packages faster to attack and exploit.

talks.title: YugabyteDB: distributed Postgres, with a database per agent and zero-copy branches
talks.summary: Yugabyte sells a distributed, PostgreSQL-compatible database and now pitches it for agents: isolated databases that scale to zero, branches to test against, and an MCP server.
key_points: Their homepage describes a multi-master database that shards automatically and fails over across zones, regions and clouds, with Postgres compatibility including stored procedures, triggers and extensions.

YugabyteDB AMP gives each agent its own Postgres database on shared infrastructure and scales idle databases to zero. It can branch a database onto separate compute, so an agent tests a change away from production.
Four built-in agents set up, migrate, tune and integrate databases; Voyager, the migration agent, handles moves from Oracle, SQL Server and MongoDB.
Their MCP server uses OIDC sign-in and keeps write tools disabled until an operator turns them on.
The core database is open source under Apache 2.0; Aeon is the managed service (per-minute or vCPU subscription), and Anywhere is self-managed. No prices appear on the pages I read.

talks.title: The Execution Muscle: Why Great Teams Are Built, Not Hired
talks.summary: A business psychologist on why projects stall on people more than code, and three daily habits that build trust, shared ownership and feedback.
key_points: In her opening poll, almost nobody said their last slipped project failed for purely technical reasons. Most hands went up for human causes like waiting on decisions or someone stuck in silence.
Her slides cite DORA 2023, where generative cultures had 30% higher organizational performance, and Google's Project Aristotle, where psychological safety was the strongest of five team dynamics.
The Relationship Bank Account treats every interaction as a deposit or withdrawal of trust. She said trust speeds up execution because every request is a withdrawal.
Deposits she named: saying you are stuck in standup, asking for review on unfinished work, owning your mistake first in the retro, and giving the reason behind a decision.
The Ownership Seesaw: when one person takes over, the others lose ownership, energy and buy-in, and the heavy lifter becomes the team's bottleneck.
Handing over ownership feels like losing control. Tight-loose-tight leadership restores it: agree the why, what done looks like, boundaries, check-ins and a say-it-back, then let go of the how.
Feedback should be regular, specific and asked for. Her SAFE structure is say what you saw, add why it matters, find out their view, and explore what is next.

talks.title: How Netflix Retrofitted Its SDLC for AI Coding Agents
talks.track: Architecting for Agents: Beneath the Loop
talks.summary: How Netflix's commerce UI team made coding agents reliable by recording one way to do each thing in the repo, then adding agents to CI and shared context.
key_points: Agents first failed on a test migration. The docs were written for people who already knew the architecture, were hard to find, and tests were written differently everywhere. Reading docs, code and tests filled a 200K-token window.
He said agents copy whatever exists, so five ways to log errors means the agent picks one. Deciding which patterns stay took the team weeks to months, and he called it the hardest part.

The team wrote about 45 architecture decision records with context, decision, pattern and anti-pattern, AI usage notes and metadata, alongside 300+ docs. Agents then migrated old code to the chosen patterns and people reviewed it.
Agents read AGENTS.md first, then a generated index of one-sentence doc summaries, then one doc in full, then the code. He compared it to robots.txt and a sitemap.

CI stays deterministic: build and lint, unit and integration tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries. The review agent posts only verified blockers with evidence, a fix and the rule; a revise label lets an agent fix the PR; nothing is auto-merged.

The review agent also flags docs a change makes stale, and about 9% of merged PRs needed a docs update. ADRs stay human-owned. After each 10% canary an RCA agent reports to on-call, who decides whether it ships.
His team's slides report zero Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and pull requests up 32% year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

For cross-service work, loading every repo, Git submodules, a Git MCP server and a shared repo all failed. Each domain now has a GraphRAG index built from AST parsing and doc extraction. One MCP tool, ask, serves it, and answers cite a file and line. Each team also has a plugin.

talks.title: Legacy as Leverage: How Brownfield Work Builds Technical Judgment
talks.summary: Shine Garg on how years of legacy work built her technical judgment, and why judgment alone couldn't stop a schema ecosystem from outgrowing its governance.
key_points: A phone in a lockbox forwarded partner signup texts to the backend. Meant as a stopgap, it ran in production for more than three years, and keeping it alive became a side job.
Automating releases across 150+ servers in 5 environments showed that redeploying an old version doesn't restore the old system after a partial failure. The deployment system became a second product.
Training, interviews, design reviews and promotion packets reward building over maintaining. Most of a system's life is the long tail after launch, often run by people who didn't build it.
For a shared messaging platform she chose SNS and SQS over Kafka and Kinesis because the team could operate it. By her figures, 3.5 years later it served 400+ engineers and 740M+ messages a day.

Adopting a technology commits the organization to expertise, tooling, monitoring, operations, hiring, training and staffing. Her slide: paved roads reduce ownership costs, and deviating should be intentional.
A sound rule that every message needs a schema grew to 2,000+ protobuf schemas in two years, with overlapping definitions of the same entity. A manual review board was disbanded within months.
She said experience made her faster at spotting decisions calcifying, not able to stop it. Changing the outcome needed ownership, incentives and organizational support.
AI makes creation cheaper while the long tail remains, so judgment becomes a stronger marker of seniority. Acting on it takes organizational and business context.
Her advice: leaders should use legacy work as training, not a dumping ground. Hiring should ask what happened 6 months later. Engineers should make the burden and their contribution visible.
She sizes legacy burden by scale, stakes, risk and cost of inaction across technical, organizational and business context. She retold her deployment project for three audiences.

talks.title: Observability: The Missing Control Plane for Agentic Engineering
talks.summary: Rachael Wonnacott on why production observability, not more tests, should decide what an AI agent may do without a human. She adds a maturity ladder for agents that use the platform directly.
key_points: Most of what gets called observability is monitoring. Her rule of thumb: if answering a new question means adding a field and redeploying, you have monitoring. OpenTelemetry solves collection, not investigation.
Self-reported maturity is far ahead of outcomes. Her slide sets 60% who call their practice mature or expert (Elastic) against 15% judged mature on outcomes such as reduced MTTR (ManageEngine).

She called observability a data discipline handed to platform engineers and app developers who weren't trained for it. The platform should own collection, defaults, storage and guardrails; app teams own what the data means. A separate observability team is an anti-pattern; embed the specialists.

Curate the shape of the data, not the questions: wide structured events, consistent field names and propagated IDs, with cost controlled by sampling healthy traffic. Telemetry is lossy under load, so measure the loss.

Agents change code, tests and the deployment harness, and aren't deterministic, so tests catch only what someone predicted. Non-deterministic systems need more rigour: canaries, flags, chaos engineering and SLOs, which few teams practise.

Shapiro's five levels measure the human and Eledath's eight levels the system around the agent; both stop at the platform edge. Her ladder adds rungs 5 to 8: the agent reads the platform, makes human-reviewed requests, gets policy-approved changes, and finally earns autonomy per capability on evidence.

Above the edge, trace the whole scenario with user, agent, tool, model, versions, scope, cost and policy decision on every span. Treat prompt, tool and model changes as releases, and score sampled production traffic against a team-owned golden set.

Specs, catalogs and change records are the as-designed state; only telemetry shows the as-built state. Reconciling the two turns each gap into a fix or a spec update, and is the evidence autonomy is granted or revoked on. Her goal is an ambient factory, not a dark one.

talks.title: You Can't Read the Code Anymore - Verifying Software in the Age of AI
talks.summary: Forter's Omer van Kloeten on reviewing behavior instead of code: agents backfill plain-English Cucumber tests into existing services, and a strict, fully faked harness makes those tests trustworthy.
key_points: Omer said verification, not authoring, is now the hard part. Reading code is harder than writing it, few people read what their agents generate, and agent-written tests mark their own homework.
He proposed reviewing what a system does rather than how it is built, using plain-English Gherkin scenarios run by Cucumber that agents write and maintain.

He listed the properties that make such tests trustworthy: black box, comprehensive (every observable behavior, citing Hyrum's Law), explicit about what must not happen, plain English, fast, deterministic and hermetic.
Forter adds a Whitebox phase after red, green, refactor, where the agent writes green tests for behavior the implementation introduced so a human can disagree with it.
Telem, Forter's skills plus deterministic tooling, backfills tests into existing code flow by flow. A billing engineer said it covered a repo in one quarter after three senior engineers had failed.
On Forter's gateway it produced about 24,700 tests across flag and configuration variations, which ran in 58.4 seconds on one laptop using in-memory fakes checked by parity tests.
A walkthrough skill explains the suite top down in HTML for review in crit; Omer said subject matter experts' surprises are a success, not a failure.

His slide put the cost at hundreds to thousands of dollars in tokens per system and 1 to 2 agent hours per flow. Human review took days for simple systems and about four engineering months for billing.

talks.title: How To Kill the Code Review
talks.summary: Aviator's Ankit Jain on keeping code review while killing line-by-line reading: agents find bugs and enforce team rules, and people review the decisions behind each change.
key_points: Ankit opened by saying he sells a replacement for code review, so the room should be suspicious of him and judge what fits its own scale.

He said review was never mostly about bugs. At Microsoft 44% of developers ranked finding defects first, but 14% of comments were about defects. Google's study of 9 million changes found the same. Review builds shared mental models.

He argued teams have already stopped reading AI-written diffs. He cited Faros figures (PRs merged with no review up 76%, incidents per month up 125%). On his own team, nine engineers merge 4x the PRs, and a person still approves each one without reading the diff.

He said AI review is noisy, but humans were never good at it either: detection falls off past about 400 lines or 60 minutes. The result is review theater. Agents write and review in a loop, and a person skims and merges.
He graded his March essay's five layers of trust. The structure was right, but no layer asked whether the team is building the right thing. He had missed human judgment.

His replacement is six verbs. Argue: agents cross-examine before the PR. Capture: intent and acceptance criteria from the session. Codify: repeated comments become enforced invariants. Prove: evidence per criterion. Debate: people review decisions, not diffs. Own: teams own the rules.

His team mined 11,400 review comments into 212 candidate rules and kept 64 invariants. Each has a rule, scope, verification method, provenance and owner. A system separate from the coding agent checks them.

He showed an incident that passed every layer: a query on a large table without an index. Rollback finished 18 minutes after impact. They asked which rule was missing, not who approved it. A year in, his team reports median time to merge of 3.4 hours, down from 2.1 days.

talks.title: Game Time: How to (Unsuccessfully) 10x in a Week & (Successfully) 10x in a Year
talks.summary: Ro's Plum Ertz on how a last-minute 2025 Super Bowl ad overwhelmed its intake site. Then a year of targets, tabletop rehearsals and queueing made the 2026 ad a non-event for the system.
key_points: In late January 2025 Ro got a last-minute streaming Super Bowl ad and about ten days to make its onboarding sites handle it. The team split the week between quick performance fixes and load testing.

They built a k6 API load test from Chrome network logs in a day and a half, against a six-week estimate. It showed the fixes helped a little and that a synchronous member UUID call was the choke point.

On the day, a logged-in user icon on the cached marketing pages made one uncacheable call per visit. That overwhelmed its service and the ingress proxy. Patients still got care, but load times reached 15 to 22 seconds and cleanup took a week.

Baseline traffic turned out to be near the system's limits. To prove a long cross-team list of changes worked together, they ran monthly tabletop sessions called D&D, Durability and Dependability, from March to May 2025, until the scenario healed itself.

Their rules for the sessions: count only what is in production, keep it to two hours, and pick curious, talkative people who know the system. Non-engineers were included, and one asked which chart says the system is safe to use.

For Super Bowl LX they set a per-service target called pathological load, from other companies' Super Bowl traffic and their own funnel. A service was done when it held the target for five minutes. Tests moved to k6 browser journeys compared day over day.

They cut the intake from about 60 API calls to the 2 it needs. A client-side request handler layer blocks unknown calls and bundles the rest into one payload. On the server, an SQS queue and a fixed pool of workers running idempotent steps flattened the spike.

They shipped in small releases with no code freeze and load tested production up to the intake database write. On game day they saw their busiest minute and hour ever, with the system at business as usual.

talks.title: AI-Assisted Coding Master Class: Build Your Mission Control
talks.summary: A half-day training. Sepehr Khosravi covered running a personal AI coding stack; Dev Bali gave a ladder of tests, from types and contracts up to formal proofs, for trusting AI-written code.
key_points: Sepehr showed his poll from last year's QCon SF: 45% of people had AI assist 0 to 25% of their coding and 14% had it do 75 to 100%. This year, by show of hands, about 70% of the room said AI did 100% of their coding. He said Copilot had been the top tool in last year's poll.

He said there are no settled practices for AI coding yet. On hard tasks he lowers the effort setting before dropping to a smaller model. He cited Anthropic cutting over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for its Claude 5 models.

He said generic skills will expire as models improve, and the skills worth keeping encode your own workflow. He summarized Anthropic's hill-climbing guide: design an eval on real tasks, validate the grader, then make one change per round and check for overfitting.
He described five software factories credited to Cole Medin (dark, fleet, PR, release and self-improving) and said he would build one to learn, not as a general recommendation.

Dev said human review was never good at catching bugs. He cited ordinary reviewers catching seeded security flaws 3% to 21% of the time, so AI review only has to beat it. Code without precise business logic can rely on AI review bots.

For code with precise business logic he gave a ladder. It starts with types and lint on every PR and contracts at every service boundary. It continues through end-to-end, property-based and mutation testing to fuzzing, symbolic execution and formal verification.

He said tests are only a gate if they are real. He cited coding agents adding mocks in 36% of commits against 26% for humans, and Meta finding 277 of 571 bug-catching tests added no line coverage. His advice: prefer properties and contracts over mocks.

He said agents are making fuzzing, property-based, symbolic and mutation testing much cheaper, but formal verification was still too slow and fragile in his own project. For most applications he concluded testing is enough.
